question: During oto-microscopy, a systematic quadrant-by-quadrant survey of the tympanic membrane is performed. Which quadrant, when found to harbour a retraction pocket or cholesteatoma, most urgently signals 'unsafe' CSOM requiring surgical intervention?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The anteroinferior quadrant is less commonly the site of dangerous pathology; perforations here are typically associated with safe tubotympanic CSOM.

Correct. Retraction pockets or perforations in the posterosuperior quadrant and pars flaccida (attic) are the hallmark of unsafe atticoantral CSOM associated with cholesteatoma, mandating surgical clearance.
The anterosuperior quadrant is not the typical site for cholesteatoma; unsafe disease predominates in the posterosuperior and attic regions.
The posteroinferior quadrant is included in safe tubotympanic perforations. While any posterior location warrants close inspection, the critical unsafe sites are posterosuperior and pars flaccida.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the CSOM safe/unsafe distinction: safe (tubotympanic) disease involves the pars tensa with a central perforation; unsafe (atticoantral) disease involves the posterosuperior pars tensa or pars flaccida, signalling cholesteatoma risk.
Well done. The posterosuperior quadrant and attic (pars flaccida) are the danger zones — retraction pockets here indicate unsafe CSOM with likely cholesteatoma.
